Kalender A.lab_name: George Thomas group, Metabolic Diseases Institute, University of Cincinnati (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Kalender A.role: Cell biologist who, in George Thomas's group at the University of Cincinnati, showed that metformin can switch off mTORC1 without AMPK by acting through the Rag GTPases
Kalender A.sub: Department of Cancer and Cell Biology and Division of Hematology-Oncology, Metabolic Diseases Institute, University of Cincinnati (papers 2010–2011, at the time of the study)
story: Adem Kalender is first author of the Atlas study KAL2010, which asked how metformin, the most widely used diabetes drug, holds back cell growth. The usual explanation was that metformin lowers cellular energy, which switches on the energy sensor AMPK, which in turn shuts down mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Kalender and colleagues tested cells that lacked AMPK or the TSC1/TSC2 brake proteins. Metformin and its stronger relative phenformin still blocked mTORC1 in those cells. What the drugs needed instead were the Rag GTPases, small switch proteins that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome when nutrients are present.

The team checked the idea in two mouse settings, one for cancer and one for diabetes, and saw the same AMPK-independent effect. Together with a liver study by Foretz and colleagues from the same year, the paper moved part of metformin's action away from the AMPK route that textbooks gave it. The work was done in cells and mice, so it says how the drug can act, not how much of its benefit in patients runs through this route.

Kalender worked in George Thomas's laboratory at the University of Cincinnati's Metabolic Diseases Institute. With Thomas, Kalender also co-wrote two short commentaries in 2010 and 2011, one on how the bending of primary cilia feeds into TOR signalling and one on how the stress kinase p38 beta connects energy stress to mTORC1. No later publications or a current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KAL2010: First author: showed in AMPK- and TSC-deficient cells and in mice that metformin and phenformin inhibit mTORC1 through the Rag GTPases rather than through AMPK.

Kalender A.note: No current position found; web search for the name gave no matching person.

Jin L.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Jin L.role: Cardiology researcher in Qiangsun Zheng's group in Xi'an who studies how metabolism and aging make the heart's upper chambers prone to atrial fibrillation
Jin L.sub: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (papers 2023–2026)
story: Lingyan Jin is first author of the Atlas study JIN2026B on rapamycin and atrial fibrillation, the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder. Its risk climbs steeply with age. To mimic aging, the team injected mice with D-galactose, a sugar that speeds up age-like damage. Rapamycin in the food lowered how easily the aged mice could be pushed into atrial fibrillation, and it eased the structural and electrical changes in the atria, the heart's upper chambers. Mitochondria worked better and the animals responded better to insulin.

The unusual part is the mechanism. Rapamycin is known as an mTOR blocker, but here the protective effect ran mainly through lower activity of HIF-1 alpha, a protein that reshapes cell metabolism when oxygen is short, and the authors describe it as independent of mTOR. This is one mouse model of accelerated aging, so it is a lead for heart rhythm research rather than evidence for treating people.

Jin's other papers come from the same Xi'an group, led by cardiologist Qiangsun Zheng with Xinghua Qin of Northwestern Polytechnical University. They treat atrial fibrillation partly as a metabolic disease: an exercise-released molecule, BAIBA, protected obese mice (2024); the metabolite succinate made mice more prone to the arrhythmia (2025); branched-chain amino acids raised the risk while swimming exercise lowered it (2025); and very hard exercise raised the risk through excess autophagy (2025). Jin also co-authored a 2024 review on how energy metabolism and the electrical activity of the atria are coupled.

highlights.JIN2026B: First author: in D-galactose-aged mice, dietary rapamycin reduced atrial fibrillation susceptibility and atrial remodelling, mainly through lower HIF-1 alpha activity rather than mTOR.

Zheng Q.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Zheng Q.role: Cardiologist at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University whose group studies atrial fibrillation as a disorder of heart metabolism, in mice and in patients
Zheng Q.sub: Department of Cardiology (Cardiovascular Medicine), The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University
story: Qiangsun Zheng is the senior author of the Atlas study JIN2026B. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular rhythm of the heart's upper chambers, becomes much more common with age. The team aged mice quickly with D-galactose injections and fed some of them rapamycin. Rapamycin lowered the animals' susceptibility to atrial fibrillation and eased the structural and electrical remodelling of the atria. It also improved mitochondrial function and insulin sensitivity. The authors traced the effect mainly to lower activity of HIF-1 alpha, a protein that switches cell metabolism under low oxygen, and described it as independent of mTOR. The evidence comes from one mouse aging model.

Zheng leads a cardiology group that works closely with Xinghua Qin's laboratory at Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi'an. Their mouse studies treat atrial fibrillation as partly a metabolic disease: a molecule released during exercise (BAIBA) protected obese mice through the energy sensor AMPK (2024), excess succinate raised the risk by harming mitochondria (2025), branched-chain amino acids raised it and swimming lowered it (2025), and very intense exercise raised it through over-active autophagy (2025). The group also studies reperfusion injury after heart attack.

On the clinical side, Zheng's recent papers look for blood markers that predict outcomes, such as an inflammation and nutrition score that forecast whether atrial fibrillation returns after catheter ablation (2026) and inflammation-related proteins in acute coronary syndrome (2026).

highlights.JIN2026B: Senior author: led the study showing that rapamycin reduced atrial fibrillation susceptibility in D-galactose-aged mice, mainly through HIF-1 alpha rather than mTOR.

Zheng Q.note: No official faculty page found; position based on consistent PubMed affiliations 2023-2026.

Su Y.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University (Tianjin, China)
Su Y.role: Cardiologist in Tianjin and Cangzhou who studied how a long non-coding RNA drives necroptotic heart-cell death after a blocked artery is reopened
Su Y.sub: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University · Department of Cardiology, Cangzhou People's Hospital, Hebei (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Yanhong Su is first author of the Atlas study SU2026, with cardiologist Jun Zhang as senior author. When a blocked heart artery is reopened, the returning blood itself causes extra damage, called ischemia-reperfusion injury. Part of that damage comes from necroptosis, a programmed form of cell death in which the cell bursts. The team looked at DLX6-AS1, a long non-coding RNA, which is an RNA molecule that regulates genes without making a protein.

In mice with ischemia-reperfusion injury, DLX6-AS1 levels rose together with the necroptosis markers RIP1, RIP3 and MLKL. In rat heart cells starved of oxygen and then re-oxygenated, extra DLX6-AS1 raised the active forms of PI3K, AKT and mTOR and made necroptosis worse, while blocking DLX6-AS1 reduced cell death. Here the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway sits on the harmful side, the opposite of many heart studies in which AKT signalling protects heart cells. The work is in mice and a rat cell line.

PubMed lists Su at the cardiology departments of Tianjin Medical University and Cangzhou People's Hospital in Hebei province. No other papers or official page could be tied to this person with confidence, so the profile rests on this study.

highlights.SU2026: First author: showed in mice and rat heart cells that the lncRNA DLX6-AS1 promotes necroptosis after ischemia-reperfusion through PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling.

Su Y.note: Only one paper could be tied to this person; current position not confirmed.

Zhang Jun.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, Cangzhou Central Hospital, Tianjin Medical University (Tianjin, China)
Zhang Jun.role: Cardiologist at Cangzhou Central Hospital, a teaching hospital of Tianjin Medical University, and senior author of a study on RNA-driven heart-cell death after reperfusion
Zhang Jun.sub: Department of Cardiology, Cangzhou Central Hospital · Tianjin Medical University (affiliations on the 2026 study)
story: Jun Zhang is the senior and corresponding author of the Atlas study SU2026, with Yanhong Su as first author. The study looked at heart damage that happens when blood flow returns after a heart artery has been blocked, known as ischemia-reperfusion injury. Some of the heart cells die by necroptosis, a programmed form of cell death in which the cell bursts open.

The team focused on DLX6-AS1, a long non-coding RNA (an RNA that regulates other genes but does not code for a protein). Its level rose in injured mouse hearts. In rat heart cells put through oxygen loss and return, more DLX6-AS1 switched on PI3K, AKT and mTOR and increased necroptosis, and blocking it reduced the damage. The results come from mice and a cell line, so they point to a possible drug target rather than a treatment.

PubMed lists Zhang at the Department of Cardiology of Cangzhou Central Hospital in Hebei province, which is affiliated with Tianjin Medical University. Jun Zhang is a very common name, and no official page could be matched with confidence, so this profile rests on the affiliation given on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SU2026: Senior author: led the study showing that DLX6-AS1 drives necroptosis through PI3K/AKT/mTOR in heart ischemia-reperfusion injury in mice and rat heart cells.

Zhang Jun.note: Very common name; profile limited to the affiliation on the Atlas paper. The paper gives Cangzhou Central Hospital (Hebei) together with a Tianjin Medical University address; location set to Tianjin as in the address line.

Bo S.lab_name: Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, Hubei University of Medicine (Xiangyang, China)
Bo S.role: Cardiothoracic surgery researcher in Xiangyang who tests natural compounds against lung cancer cells, including gambogic acid acting on the AKT and mTOR pathway
Bo S.sub: Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, affiliated with Hubei University of Medicine (papers 2021–2026)
story: Su Bo is first author of the Atlas study BO2026, which tested gambogic acid, a yellow compound from the resin of the gamboge tree, on lung cancer cells. The study had two parts. In the computer part, network pharmacology and molecular docking (a simulation of how well a molecule fits into a protein) suggested that gambogic acid binds most tightly to AKT and to S6K1, a kinase that mTORC1 switches on to drive growth. In the lab part, the compound killed A549 lung cancer cells and pushed them into apoptosis, a controlled form of cell death.

The study did not measure whether gambogic acid directly blocks the mTOR enzyme, and it had no animal or human data. Docking predicts possible binding but does not prove it, so the link to mTOR remains a hypothesis to test.

PubMed lists Bo at the Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery of Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital, a hospital of Hubei University of Medicine. An earlier paper from the same department (2021) followed the same approach with purpurin, another plant-derived compound, which killed A549 lung cancer cells through oxidative stress and lower PI3K/AKT signalling. No official profile page was found.

highlights.BO2026: First author: combined docking with cell experiments to show that gambogic acid kills A549 lung cancer cells and is predicted to bind AKT and S6K1.

Bo S.note: Name order: PubMed gives surname Bo, given name Su; displayed as Su Bo.

Lane CM.lab_name: Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)
Lane CM.role: Cardiologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, working in interventional cardiology, and first author of a trial of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Lane CM.sub: Department of Cardiovascular Medicine (Division of Interventional Cardiology), Mayo Clinic, Rochester (2023–2026) · Department of Internal Medicine, Mayo Clinic (2020–2021)
story: Conor Lane is first author of the Atlas entry LAN2026, a 2026 Mayo Clinic Proceedings report on rapamycin in frail older people who have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). In HFpEF the heart pumps out a normal share of its blood with each beat but is stiff and fills poorly. It is common in older adults, and there are few treatments that help. Rapamycin, the classic mTOR blocker, slows aging processes in animals, so a trial in this group tests whether that idea carries over to a real age-related disease in people.

The team joined Mayo Clinic cardiologists, including senior author Mandeep Singh, with aging researchers James Kirkland at Mayo and Dudley Lamming and Judith Simcox at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The abstract was not yet public when the Atlas entry was made, so the results are not summarised here.

Lane's other papers trace a clinical career at Mayo Clinic in Rochester. In 2020 and 2021 PubMed lists the Department of Internal Medicine, on studies of heart ultrasound methods and of medicines linked to microscopic colitis. From 2023 the affiliation is cardiovascular medicine, with case reports and commentary on catheter-based treatments, such as removing infected material from a mitral valve, repairing a coronary aneurysm and opening a blocked bypass graft. By 2025 Lane is listed in the Division of Interventional Cardiology.

highlights.LAN2026: First author of the Mayo Clinic and University of Wisconsin report on low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with HFpEF.

Lane CM.note: LAN2026 abstract still not available; check results when published. Current position inferred from PubMed affiliations only (no official page opened; web search budget exhausted).

Holz MK.lab_name: Department of Cell and Molecular Physiology, Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, New York Medical College (Valhalla, New York, USA)
Holz MK.role: Cell biologist who, as a postdoc with John Blenis, showed how mTOR and S6K1 trade places on eIF3 to start protein synthesis, and who now studies mTOR in breast cancer and the rare lung disease LAM at New York Medical College
Holz MK.sub: Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences and Department of Cell and Molecular Physiology, New York Medical College (2026) · Department of Cell Biology and Anatomy, New York Medical College (from 2018) · Department of Biology, Stern College for Women, Yeshiva University, and Albert Einstein Cancer Center (papers to 2017) · Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, John Blenis lab (2005)
story: Marina Holz is first author of the Atlas study HOL2005, done in John Blenis's lab at Harvard Medical School. It answered a basic question: how does mTOR, once switched on by growth signals, get the cell's protein-making machinery started? The answer centred on eIF3, a large protein platform that helps ribosomes find the start of a messenger RNA. In resting cells the kinase S6K1 sits on eIF3 in an inactive state. When the cell is stimulated, mTOR arrives with its partner raptor, phosphorylates S6K1, and S6K1 lets go of eIF3 to phosphorylate its own targets, which helps assemble the complex that begins translation. The paper turned a list of phosphorylation events into an ordered sequence on one scaffold. It was done in cultured human cells.

After Harvard, Holz set up a lab in the Department of Biology at Stern College for Women of Yeshiva University, with a link to the Albert Einstein Cancer Center. The group studied how estrogen and mTOR signalling feed each other in breast cancer: mTOR and S6K1 together with the MAPK pathway phosphorylate estrogen receptor alpha (2010), estrogen raises S6K1 levels in a loop that drives breast cancer cell growth (2012), and estrogen tunes the eIF3 subunit eIF3f through mTORC1 (2018).

A second line of work is lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a rare lung disease of women caused by overactive mTORC1. In mice carrying TSC2-deficient tumours, rapamycin combined with resveratrol switched on cell death (2015), and Holz was senior author of a small clinical study of resveratrol plus sirolimus in LAM patients (2023). At New York Medical College in Valhalla, Holz's recent papers report that CDK4/6 inhibitors suppress mTOR activity in LAM cells (2026) and that education level affects how quickly LAM patients are diagnosed and treated (2026).

highlights.HOL2005: First author: showed in cultured cells that mTOR/raptor and S6K1 swap places on the eIF3 complex in an ordered sequence that starts translation.

Please check whether HOL2005 carries a correction or expression of concern. Holz's exact title at New York Medical College (for example any dean role) not confirmed from an official page.

Schalm SS.role: Cell biologist who, in John Blenis's lab, showed that the TOS motif lets raptor grab 4E-BP1 so mTORC1 can phosphorylate it, and who later moved into cancer drug discovery in the biotech industry
Schalm SS.sub: Kymera Therapeutics, Watertown (2025 paper) · Blueprint Medicines, Cambridge, Massachusetts (2022 paper) · Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Harvard University, Tom Maniatis lab (2010) · Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, John Blenis lab (2000–2004)
story: Stefanie Schalm is first author of the Atlas study SCH2003 from John Blenis's lab at Harvard Medical School. It explains how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, recognises one of its main targets. 4E-BP1 is a brake on protein synthesis: while unphosphorylated it holds on to eIF4E, the factor that binds the cap at the start of a messenger RNA. Once mTORC1 adds several phosphate groups, 4E-BP1 lets go and translation can begin.

The paper showed that a short stretch at the end of 4E-BP1, the TOR signalling (TOS) motif, is what binds raptor, the partner protein that hands substrates to mTOR. Without a working TOS motif, raptor could not bind 4E-BP1 and the multiple phosphorylation steps failed, so 4E-BP1 kept blocking translation. It established the TOS motif as a docking signal on 4E-BP1 for mTORC1. The experiments were done in cultured cells.

With Blenis, Schalm also co-wrote a 2004 review on how the PI3-kinase and TOR pathways join to control cell growth. By 2010 PubMed lists Schalm in Tom Maniatis's group in Harvard's Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, studying how the receptor kinase Ret phosphorylates protocadherins, adhesion proteins of nerve cells. Later papers list Blueprint Medicines (2022), on a kinase inhibitor approach for fibrolamellar liver cancer, and Kymera Therapeutics (2025), on a drug that degrades the p53 inhibitor MDM2.

highlights.SCH2003: First author: showed in cultured cells that the TOS motif of 4E-BP1 mediates raptor binding and is needed for its multisite phosphorylation by mTORC1.

Schalm SS.note: Industry positions (Blueprint Medicines 2022, Kymera Therapeutics 2025) come from PubMed affiliations only; the name is uncommon and the field (kinase signalling) matches, but no official page was opened.

Petit CS.lab_name: Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Petit CS.role: Cell biologist who showed, in Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale, that folliculin moves onto lysosomes when amino acids run out and is needed to switch on the Rag GTPases
Petit CS.sub: Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Farese and Walther lab (2020, most recent paper) · Department of Cell Biology, Yale University School of Medicine, Shawn Ferguson lab (2012–2013) · Centre de Recherche des Cordeliers, Paris, Sophie Thenet group (2008–2013)
story: Constance Petit is first author of the Atlas study PET2013 from Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, when amino acids are available. Small switch proteins called Rag GTPases do the recruiting. The open question was which protein flips the Rags into their active state.

Petit and colleagues found that folliculin (FLCN), the protein lost in the inherited Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, gathers on lysosomes when amino acids are withdrawn and binds RagA directly. Cells without folliculin could not recruit mTORC1 to lysosomes when amino acids were added back. This placed folliculin at the amino acid switch of mTORC1. The study used cultured human cells. Petit was also a co-author on the 2012 Ferguson lab paper showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates the transcription factor TFEB at lysosomes (ROC2012).

Before Yale, Petit worked in Sophie Thenet's group at the Centre de Recherche des Cordeliers in Paris on the cellular prion protein and the junctions that seal the gut lining, including a 2012 study on its role in the intestinal barrier and in inflammatory bowel disease. In 2020 PubMed lists Petit as first author in Robert Farese and Tobias Walther's lab at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, showing that blocking sphingolipid synthesis improved survival in a mouse model of motor neuron degeneration. No later position could be confirmed.

highlights.PET2013: First author: showed in human cells that folliculin moves to lysosomes on amino acid withdrawal, binds RagA and is needed for amino acid-driven mTORC1 recruitment.

Petit CS.note: Current position not confirmed; last PubMed affiliation 2020 (Harvard T.H. Chan). Paris work may be PhD training but no thesis record was checked.

Roczniak-Ferguson A.lab_name: Ferguson Lab, Department of Cell Biology, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Roczniak-Ferguson A.role: Cell biologist in Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale who showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates the transcription factor TFEB to control lysosome and autophagy genes, and who studies lysosome biology in neurodegenerative disease
Roczniak-Ferguson A.sub: Department of Cell Biology and Program in Cellular Neuroscience, Neurodegeneration and Repair, Yale University School of Medicine (2012–2026) · Department of Cancer Biology, Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, Albert Reynolds lab (2003–2004)
story: Agnes Roczniak-Ferguson is first author of the Atlas study ROC2012 from Shawn Ferguson's lab at Yale. TFEB is a transcription factor, a protein that turns on a set of genes, in this case the genes that build lysosomes and run autophagy, the cell's self-recycling process. The study showed that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, phosphorylates TFEB on the lysosome surface. This keeps TFEB from switching on its target genes. When mTORC1 is switched off, for example by starvation, TFEB becomes active and lysosome and autophagy genes are turned on.

The result tied the same nutrient signal that drives growth to the building of the cell's recycling system: when food is plentiful mTORC1 holds TFEB back, and when it is scarce the cell can build more lysosomes. It was done in cultured human cells.

Earlier, at Vanderbilt University, Roczniak-Ferguson studied p120-catenin, a protein that controls cell-cell adhesion, with Albert Reynolds (2003, 2004). At Yale Roczniak-Ferguson has stayed with lysosome biology in the Ferguson lab: C9orf72, the gene most often mutated in ALS and frontotemporal dementia, binds SMCR8 and affects mTORC1 responses to amino acids (2016); loss of TDP-43 disturbs many organelles (2019); and the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 is switched on at damaged lysosomes through the STING, CASM and GABARAP pathway (2025) and through the chloride transporter ClC-7 (2026).

highlights.ROC2012: First author: showed in human cells that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB to control the transcription of lysosome and autophagy genes.

Roczniak-Ferguson A.note: Exact job title in the Ferguson lab not confirmed from an official page.

Nelson JF.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Nelson JF.role: Physiologist of aging at UT Health San Antonio who studies how calorie restriction, sex hormones and drugs change mouse lifespan, and a co-investigator on the Interventions Testing Program
Nelson JF.sub: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2003–2026)
story: James Nelson is a co-author of the Atlas study STR2022 from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program (ITP). The ITP tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at the same time, so a result has to hold up in different labs. In this cohort, male mice given rapamycin together with acarbose, a drug that slows sugar uptake from the gut, starting at 9 months of age lived longer than males on rapamycin alone in earlier ITP cohorts. In females the combination was neither better nor worse than rapamycin alone. The drug captopril also gave a small lifespan gain. All of this is in mice.

Nelson's own research at the Barshop Institute asks why some interventions slow aging and why the sexes differ. Nelson's group found that how well a mouse keeps its body fat predicts whether dietary restriction will lengthen its life (2011), that the higher stress-hormone levels of calorie-restricted mice help explain their lower inflammation (2019), and that castration before puberty removed the lifespan difference between male and female mice (2023).

As part of the San Antonio ITP team, Nelson is a co-author on many of the program's reports, including the 2016 study in which acarbose, an antioxidant and other compounds lengthened male lifespan, the 2021 report that 17-alpha-estradiol given late in life helped male mice, and a 2026 report of eight compounds that did not extend lifespan.

highlights.STR2022: Co-author from the San Antonio ITP site: rapamycin plus acarbose from 9 months gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts.

Nelson JF.note: Current faculty title not confirmed from an official page (web search budget exhausted); affiliation consistent in PubMed through 2026.

Diaz V.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Diaz V.role: Aging researcher at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio who has worked for more than a decade on the mouse lifespan studies behind rapamycin's reputation as an anti-aging drug, including the Interventions Testing Program
Diaz V.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2013–2026)
story: Vivian Diaz is a co-author of two Atlas studies from San Antonio. In FOK2014, mice fed rapamycin lived longer, and their livers showed large changes in which genes were switched on, a first look at what long-term rapamycin does inside an organ. In STR2022, from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which tests drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites, male mice given rapamycin plus acarbose from 9 months of age lived longer than males on rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts, while in females the combination matched rapamycin alone. Both studies are in mice.

PubMed lists Diaz at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio on a long run of mouse aging studies. Diaz is also a co-author on ITP reports on canagliflozin (2020) and on epicatechin, halofuginone and mitoglitazone (2025), and on a 2026 Nature study of genetic and body-wide trade-offs in aging and mortality.
These papers show steady work on the San Antonio mouse aging studies; Diaz's exact role in the team was not stated in the sources checked.

highlights.FOK2014: Co-author: mice fed rapamycin lived longer and showed large changes in the liver transcriptome.
highlights.STR2022: Co-author from the San Antonio ITP site: rapamycin plus acarbose from 9 months gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts.

Marchant ED.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Long School of Medicine, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Marchant ED.role: Muscle physiologist in the Rasmussen group in San Antonio who studies what overactive mTORC1 in skeletal muscle does to metabolism, inflammation and exercise adaptation
Marchant ED.sub: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Long School of Medicine, and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (2024–2026) · Department of Nutrition, Dietetics, and Food Science, Brigham Young University (papers 2018–2022)
story: Erik Marchant is first author of the Atlas study MARCHANT2026, with B. B. Rasmussen as senior author. Overactive mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in muscle is often linked with insulin resistance, the state in which the body handles sugar poorly. To test whether one causes the other, the team switched mTORC1 on permanently in mouse skeletal muscle by removing GATOR1, a protein complex that normally turns mTORC1 off when amino acids are scarce.

The muscles showed more signs of inflammation, but the mice still handled a glucose load normally. So muscle mTORC1 overactivity alone was not enough to cause glucose intolerance, and other metabolic inputs must be needed. A companion paper from the same group in 2026, with Marchant as second author, found that this kind of hyperactive muscle mTORC1 blunted the benefits of endurance training even though mitochondria and lipids changed. Both studies are in mice.

Before San Antonio, Marchant published from the Department of Nutrition, Dietetics, and Food Science at Brigham Young University in Utah, including a 2020 study showing that, unlike a high-fat diet, bed rest did not appear to cause insulin resistance through mitochondrial oxidants, and a 2018 commentary on restricting branched-chain amino acids for metabolic health. In San Antonio Marchant has also co-authored human studies of muscle disuse and rehabilitation in middle-aged adults (2025) and of PDE-5 inhibitors (2026).

highlights.MARCHANT2026: First author: showed that permanently active mTORC1 in mouse skeletal muscle, made by deleting GATOR1, raises inflammation but does not by itself impair glucose tolerance.

Marchant ED.note: The Atlas paper gives 'University of Texas at San Antonio, Long School of Medicine' (UT Health San Antonio became part of UTSA); lab_name uses UT Health San Antonio. Job title (postdoc or faculty) not confirmed. A Nathan D. Marchant at BYU is a different person.

Feldman ME.lab_name: Shokat lab, Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, UCSF and Howard Hughes Medical Institute (San Francisco, California, USA)
Feldman ME.role: Chemical biologist who, in the Shokat lab at UCSF, introduced PP242 and the TORKinib class of drugs that block mTOR's active site and reach the outputs rapamycin misses
Feldman ME.sub: Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology and Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California San Francisco, Shokat lab (papers 2006–2012, at the time of the study)
story: Morris Feldman is first author of the Atlas study FEL2009 from the Shokat lab at UCSF. Rapamycin does not bind mTOR's active site. It sticks to the side of mTORC1 and blocks only some of its outputs, and it barely touches the second complex, mTORC2. Feldman and colleagues made small molecules called TORKinibs, including PP242 and PP30, that sit in the ATP pocket of the mTOR kinase itself. These hit both complexes.

The key result was that active-site inhibitors shut down cap-dependent translation, the main way cells start making proteins, much more strongly than rapamycin. A parallel study by Thoreen and colleagues reported the same conclusion in the same year. Together the two papers opened a new class of mTOR drugs beyond rapamycin and its analogues. The work was done in cultured cells.

PP242 then became a common research tool. Feldman is a co-author on several papers that used it, including the 2012 Nature study from the Ruggero group showing that mTOR-controlled translation steers cancer initiation and metastasis, a 2010 study showing that mTORC2 activates the kidney sodium channel ENaC through SGK1, a 2010 study of a herpesvirus protein that keeps mTORC1 switched on, and a 2012 study combining active-site mTOR inhibitors with chemotherapy for colorectal cancer. No current position could be confirmed.

highlights.FEL2009: First author: developed the active-site mTOR inhibitors PP242 and PP30 and showed they block rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1 and mTORC2, including cap-dependent translation.

Feldman ME.note: PubMed also lists a Morris E. Feldman at the Weizmann Institute (Yosef Yarden lab, 2014 and 2017) working on growth-factor signalling; likely the same person but not confirmed by a shared collaborator, so left out of the story.

Fok WC.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Structural Biology and Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Fok WC.role: Biologist of aging who, in Viviana Pérez's group in San Antonio, compared rapamycin with dietary restriction in mouse liver and showed that rapamycin's lifespan gain comes with large changes in liver gene activity
Fok WC.sub: Department of Cellular and Structural Biology and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2012–2015, at the time of the study)
story: Wilson Fok is first author of the Atlas study FOK2014, with A. Richardson as senior author. Mice fed rapamycin in their food lived longer, and their livers showed large changes in which genes were turned on or off, measured across the whole transcriptome. The study helped connect rapamycin's effect on lifespan with concrete changes in an organ that controls much of the body's metabolism. It is a mouse study.

Fok's other first-author papers from San Antonio, with Viviana Pérez, compared rapamycin with dietary restriction, the best-known way to extend lifespan in lab animals. Short-term treatment in young mice showed that the two had overlapping but distinct effects (2012), and combining them changed the liver transcriptome and metabolome more than either alone (2013). Fok was also a co-author on a 2014 study showing that rapamycin and dietary restriction cause metabolically distinct changes in mouse liver.

In 2015 Fok is listed at the Barshop Institute on a study of a mitochondrial protease in muscle cells. No later position could be confirmed from sources that tie directly to this work, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.FOK2014: First author: showed that rapamycin-fed mice lived longer and had large changes in the liver transcriptome.

Fok WC.note: PubMed lists a Wilson Chun Fok at Washington University in St. Louis (Luis Batista lab, 2017-2023, telomeres and dyskeratosis congenita). Probably the same person (uncommon name) but no shared collaborator with the San Antonio work, so not included. Please confirm if wanted.

Sang Z.lab_name: Jie Wang group, Department of Chemistry, Southern University of Science and Technology (Shenzhen, China)
Sang Z.role: Chemical biologist at SUSTech in Shenzhen who used a light-activated methionine probe to identify PKM2 as a methionine sensor for mTORC1
Sang Z.sub: Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis and State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Southern University of Science and Technology (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Zixin Sang is first author of the Atlas study SANG2026, from Jie Wang's group in the Department of Chemistry at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only runs when amino acids are available, and cells have dedicated sensor proteins that report each amino acid. For methionine the known sensor, SAMTOR, does not read methionine itself but a product made from it, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). Whether any protein reads free methionine directly was an open question.

Sang and colleagues built a "Trojan" methionine: a copy of the amino acid that cells take up normally but that carries a chemical group which, when hit with light, links the probe to whatever protein is holding it. Fishing out these proteins with chemoproteomics, a method that identifies protein targets of small molecules on a large scale, pointed to PKM2. PKM2 is best known as a glycolysis enzyme, but here it bound methionine through a separate pocket, independently of its enzyme activity, and passed the signal to mTORC1 through the GATOR2 complex. The work was done in cultured cells and complements SAMTOR rather than replacing it.

PubMed lists Sang at the Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis and State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics at SUSTech. No other papers or an official page could be tied to this person, so the profile rests on this study.

highlights.SANG2026: First author: used a photo-crosslinking methionine probe and chemoproteomics to show that PKM2 binds methionine and relays it to mTORC1 through GATOR2.

Sang Z.note: Only one paper; career stage (student or postdoc) not confirmed.

Chung CL.lab_name: Montgomery Dermatology and Lankenau Institute for Medical Research (Wynnewood, Pennsylvania, USA)
Chung CL.role: Dermatologist specialising in skin disease of organ transplant recipients, and first author of a small randomised trial showing that topical rapamycin lowers a senescence marker in aging human skin
Chung CL.sub: Montgomery Dermatology and Lankenau Institute for Medical Research, Pennsylvania (papers 2019–2026) · Department of Dermatology, Drexel University College of Medicine, Philadelphia (papers 2012–2019)
story: Christina Lee Chung is first author of the Atlas study CHU2019, with Christian Sell of Drexel University as senior author. Skin is a good place to test an anti-aging drug in people, because it can be seen, photographed and sampled with a small biopsy. In this exploratory randomised trial, older adults were randomised to rapamycin or placebo skin cream. Rapamycin lowered p16, a marker of senescent cells (old cells that have stopped dividing and send out inflammatory signals), and raised collagen VII, a protein that anchors the skin layers. Some participants' skin also looked better.

The trial was small: 36 people enrolled and 17 completed it. So it is early evidence that topical rapamycin can reduce a senescence marker in human skin, not proof that it slows skin aging. It is one of the few human studies in the Atlas in which rapamycin was applied to a tissue rather than given as a pill.

Chung's clinical research centres on skin disease in organ transplant recipients, who take drugs that suppress the immune system and develop skin cancers far more often than other people. At Drexel Chung led studies comparing skin disease after transplant across racial groups (2017) and on genital lesions in transplant recipients (2018). Later papers list Montgomery Dermatology and the Lankenau Institute for Medical Research in Pennsylvania, including expert consensus work on skin cancer screening and prevention after transplant (2019, 2021) and on topical treatment of precancerous skin lesions (2026).

highlights.CHU2019: First author: ran the randomised trial in which topical rapamycin lowered p16 and raised collagen VII in aging human skin.

Chung CL.note: Post-Drexel affiliation (Montgomery Dermatology / Lankenau Institute) from PubMed only; same full name and same transplant-dermatology niche.

Covey DF.lab_name: Department of Developmental Biology and Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research, Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, Missouri, USA)
Covey DF.role: Medicinal chemist at Washington University in St. Louis who designs synthetic steroids and sterols, used to study neurosteroids, GABA-A receptors and cholesterol sensing, including in two Atlas studies on cholesterol and mTORC1
Covey DF.sub: Department of Developmental Biology and Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis
story: Douglas Covey is a co-author of two Atlas studies from the Zoncu lab on how lysosomes tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that cholesterol is available. In CAS2017 the team showed that cholesterol in the lysosome membrane switches on mTORC1. The transporter SLC38A9 is needed for this through cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein, separate from its role in sensing arginine, while NPC1, the protein that exports cholesterol out of the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. In SHI2022 they found a second sensor, LYCHOS (formerly called GPR155). When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS binds GATOR1, a brake on mTORC1, and takes it out of action, so mTORC1 can be recruited to the lysosome. Both studies were done mainly in cultured cells.

Covey's own field is the chemistry of steroids and sterols. Covey's group at Washington University makes modified versions of these molecules and tests how small changes in shape alter what they do. Much of this work, often with Mennerick, concerns neurosteroids, natural brain steroids that act on GABA-A receptors, the main inhibitory receptors of the brain, and their potential for treating psychiatric disorders. Recent papers use machine learning and screening to find new neurosteroid targets (2025), test steroid and sterol analogues on inflammation in brain immune cells (2026) and show that flipping the orientation of one hydroxy group in cholesterol changes how the molecule moves inside cells (2026).
PubMed lists Covey at the Department of Developmental Biology and the Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research at Washington University School of Medicine.

highlights.CAS2017: Co-author: lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9, and NPC1 restrains this signal.
highlights.SHI2022: Co-author: identified LYCHOS as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor that releases mTORC1 by binding GATOR1.

Covey DF.note: Covey's specific contribution to CAS2017 and SHI2022 not stated in sources seen; story does not state it. Academic rank not confirmed from an official page.

Poulsen MM.lab_name: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital (Aarhus, Denmark)
Poulsen MM.role: Endocrinologist at Aarhus University Hospital who led one of the first careful human trials of high-dose resveratrol, which found no metabolic benefit in obese men
Poulsen MM.sub: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital (papers 2012–2025)
story: Morten Møller Poulsen is first author of the Atlas study POU2013, with Jens Otto Lunde Jørgensen as senior author. Resveratrol, a compound found in red grape skin, had made headlines because it seemed to mimic calorie restriction and protect rodents on rich diets. Poulsen and colleagues gave obese but otherwise healthy men a high dose of resveratrol or a placebo for four weeks and measured insulin sensitivity, fuel use, blood pressure and body composition with precise methods.

Resveratrol changed none of them. The result contradicted the rodent data that had driven the enthusiasm and is a useful reminder that a strong animal result does not guarantee a human one. The trial was short and small, so it cannot rule out effects with longer treatment, but it set a clear benchmark.

Poulsen's earlier work in the same Aarhus group, with Pedersen as senior author, tested resveratrol in rats on a high-fat diet, where it prevented fatty liver (2012), and the group later reported that resveratrol also did not help people with the metabolic syndrome (2017). More recent papers from the Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine follow Danish families with RET gene variants that cause multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, an inherited cancer syndrome of the thyroid and adrenal glands, in nationwide studies (2019 to 2025).

highlights.POU2013: First author: ran the randomised trial in which four weeks of high-dose resveratrol had no effect on insulin sensitivity, blood pressure or body composition in obese men.

Poulsen MM.note: Full name with middle name from PubMed (Morten Møller Poulsen).

Jørgensen JO.lab_name: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital, and Department of Clinical Medicine, Aarhus University (Aarhus, Denmark)
Jørgensen JO.role: Endocrinologist at Aarhus University whose research centres on growth hormone and metabolism in people, and senior author of a trial showing that high-dose resveratrol did not improve metabolism in obese men
Jørgensen JO.sub: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital · Department of Clinical Medicine, Aarhus University
story: Jens Otto Lunde Jørgensen is the senior author of the Atlas study POU2013, with Morten Møller Poulsen as first author. Resveratrol, a compound from grape skins, had looked promising in rodents, where it seemed to copy some effects of calorie restriction. The Aarhus team tested it properly in people: obese men took a high dose or a placebo for four weeks, and the researchers measured insulin sensitivity, how the body burned fuel, blood pressure and body composition.

None of these changed with resveratrol. The trial was short and small, but it was carefully controlled, and it showed that the rodent results did not carry over to this group of people. A later trial from the same Aarhus groups, with Jørgensen as a co-author, found no benefit of resveratrol in the metabolic syndrome either (2017).

Jørgensen's main research line is growth hormone, the pituitary hormone that drives growth in children and shapes fat, muscle and sugar metabolism in adults. The group studies how the hormone acts in muscle and fat, including in people with acromegaly, the condition caused by too much growth hormone. Recent papers show that excess growth hormone causes reversible scarring (fibrosis) in muscle and fat of patients with acromegaly (2026) and compare methods for measuring body composition in acromegaly (2025). A 2014 study from the resveratrol trial examined growth hormone signalling in muscle and fat of obese people.

highlights.POU2013: Senior author: led the randomised trial in which four weeks of high-dose resveratrol did not change insulin sensitivity, blood pressure or body composition in obese men.

Jørgensen JO.note: Academic title (professor) not confirmed from an official page; web search budget was exhausted.

He Y.lab_name: Xuefeng Yu group, Division of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
He Y.role: Endocrinology researcher in Xuefeng Yu's group at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan who studies the liver- and fat-derived hormone ANGPTL8 in aging and diabetes
He Y.sub: Division of Endocrinology, Department of Internal Medicine, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (papers 2024–2026)
story: Yi He is first author of the Atlas study HE2026, with Xuefeng Yu as senior author. ANGPTL8 is a hormone-like protein released into the blood that helps control fat and sugar metabolism. In a large human cohort, higher ANGPTL8 levels went along with an older biological age and a higher risk of death. In mice, deleting the Angptl8 gene lengthened life and lowered markers of senescence, the state in which cells stop dividing and release inflammatory signals.

The team traced the mechanism in fat tissue. ANGPTL8 binds AKT2, a kinase in the insulin pathway, and drives the AKT-mTOR-S6K chain that pushes fat cells into senescence; blocking that chain removed the effect. The human data are associations, while cause and mechanism come from mice and cells, so ANGPTL8 is a candidate driver of fat-tissue aging rather than a proven one in people.

Yi He's other papers come from the same Tongji endocrinology group and follow ANGPTL8 into other organs: it steers bone marrow stem cells towards fat instead of bone during skeletal aging (2025), it drives inflammation and scarring in kidney tubule cells in diabetic kidney disease through AKT2 (2025), and blocking it protected against diabetes-related memory problems in mice (2024).

highlights.HE2026: First author: linked circulating ANGPTL8 to biological age in people and showed in mice that it drives fat-cell senescence through AKT2 and mTOR-S6K.

He Y.note: Very common name; only papers from the Tongji Division of Endocrinology with Xuefeng Yu were used. A Yi He in Tongji cardiology (PMIDs 39857701, 40242212, 42571818) is a different person and was excluded. Career stage not confirmed.

Liang X.lab_name: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
Liang X.role: Toxicology and environmental health researcher who found that the long non-coding RNA LINP1 protects skin cells from radiation-induced senescence by binding mTOR
Liang X.sub: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (2026) · Department of Toxicology, School of Public Health, Southern Medical University, Guangzhou (2025)
story: Xiaoting Liang is first author of the Atlas study LIANG2026, with Liang Zhou of Southern Medical University in Guangzhou as senior author. Radiotherapy often damages the skin, and part of that damage comes from senescence, the state in which cells stop dividing for good. The team found that LINP1, a long non-coding RNA (an RNA that regulates other molecules without making a protein), rises sharply in keratinocytes, the main cells of the outer skin, after radiation.

LINP1 binds the FAT domain of mTOR through a central stretch of the RNA. This weakens the contact between mTOR and the tumour suppressor p53, so less p53 is phosphorylated at serine 15, and the cells are less likely to become senescent. Removing LINP1 made radiation damage worse in cultured keratinocytes and in pieces of human skin kept alive in the lab. Here mTOR acts as a partner of p53 in the stress response, not as a nutrient sensor.

Before moving to Shanxi Medical University in Taiyuan, Liang was listed at the Department of Toxicology of Southern Medical University's School of Public Health, as a co-author with Zhou on a 2025 study of how another long non-coding RNA drives drug resistance in melanoma.

highlights.LIANG2026: First author: showed in keratinocytes and human skin explants that LINP1 binds mTOR, reduces p53 Ser15 phosphorylation and limits radiation-induced senescence.

Liang X.note: Two other PubMed hits for this name (PMID 41204209, Shanxi HIV testing; PMID 31789413, Shanghai) not used, identity unclear.

Ren Y.lab_name: Yanfeng Hu group, Department of General Surgery, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China)
Ren Y.role: Gastric cancer researcher in Yanfeng Hu's surgical group at Nanfang Hospital who studies how tumour bacteria and metabolism shape resistance to immunotherapy
Ren Y.sub: Department of General Surgery and Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (papers 2023–2026)
story: Yingxin Ren is first author of the Atlas study REN2026, with Yanfeng Hu as senior author. Immune checkpoint drugs that block PD-1 release a brake on T cells so they can attack tumours, but many gastric cancers do not respond. The team linked part of this resistance to bacteria living inside the tumour. Streptococcus anginosus was associated with kynurenic acid, a metabolite that raised levels of the integrin ITGA2 in cancer cells.

ITGA2 then held back an mTOR-dependent cascade, which kept cathepsin V (CTSV) expression high and weakened the killing activity of CD8 T cells. In this setting lower mTOR activity sits on the side of immune escape, a reminder that the effect of mTOR depends on cell type and context.

Ren's other papers come from the same group and the Guangdong key laboratory for gastrointestinal tumours: tumour bacteria and their vesicles that improve PD-1 therapy (2026), gut bacteria that tune CD8 T cell immunity through butyrate (2024), an enzyme that protects gastric cancer stem cells from ferroptosis through a cholesterol and mTOR pathway (2024), and imaging probes for lymph nodes and peritoneal spread (2025, 2026).

highlights.REN2026: First author: showed that tumour-associated kynurenic acid drives PD-1 blockade resistance in gastric cancer through an ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis that suppresses CD8 T cells.
